31:29.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُولِجُ ٱلَّيۡلَ فِي ٱلنَّهَارِ وَيُولِجُ ٱلنَّهَارَ فِي ٱلَّيۡلِ وَسَخَّرَ ٱلشَّمۡسَ وَٱلۡقَمَرَۖ كُلࣱّ يَجۡرِيٓ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلࣲ مُّسَمࣰّ ى وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ خَبِيرࣱ‏
31:29.en: Hast thou not seen how Allah causeth the night to pass into the day and causeth the day to pass into the night, and hath subdued the sun and the moon (to do their work), each running unto an appointed term; and that Allah is Informed of what ye do

31:30.ar: ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلۡحَقُّ وَأَنَّ مَا يَدۡعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ ٱلۡبَٰطِلُ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلۡعَلِيُّ ٱلۡكَبِيرُ
31:30.en: That (is so) because Allah, He is the True, and that which they invoke beside Him is the False, and because Allah, He is the Sublime, the Great

31:31.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱلۡفُلۡكَ تَجۡرِي فِي ٱلۡبَحۡرِ بِنِعۡمَتِ ٱللَّهِ لِيُرِيَكُم مِّنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦٓۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّكُلِّ صَبَّارࣲ شَكُورࣲ‏
31:31.en: Hast thou not seen how the ships glide on the sea by Allah's grace, that He may show you of His wonders? Lo! therein indeed are portents for every steadfast, grateful (heart)

31:32.ar: وَإِذَا غَشِيَهُم مَّوۡجࣱ كَٱلظُّلَلِ دَعَوُاْ ٱللَّهَ مُخۡلِصِينَ لَهُ ٱلدِّينَ فَلَمَّا نَجَّىٰهُمۡ إِلَى ٱلۡبَرِّ فَمِنۡهُم مُّقۡتَصِدࣱۚ وَمَا يَجۡحَدُ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَآ إِلَّا كُلُّ خَتَّارࣲ كَفُورࣲ‏
31:32.en: And if a wave enshroudeth them like awnings, they cry unto Allah, making their faith pure for Him only. But when He bringeth them safe to land, some of them compromise. None denieth Our signs save every traitor ingrate

31:33.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱتَّقُواْ رَبَّكُمۡ وَٱخۡشَوۡاْ يَوۡمࣰ ا لَّا يَجۡزِي وَالِدٌ عَن وَلَدِهِۦ وَلَا مَوۡلُودٌ هُوَ جَازٍ عَن وَالِدِهِۦ شَيۡـًٔاۚ إِنَّ وَعۡدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقࣱّۖ فَلَا تَغُرَّنَّكُمُ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَلَا يَغُرَّنَّكُم بِٱللَّهِ ٱلۡغَرُورُ
31:33.en: O mankind! Keep your duty to your Lord and fear a Day when the parent will not be able to avail the child in aught, nor the child to avail the parent. Lo! Allah's promise is the very truth. Let not the life of the world beguile you, nor let the deceiver beguile you, in regard to Allah

31:34.ar: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عِندَهُۥ عِلۡمُ ٱلسَّاعَةِ وَيُنَزِّلُ ٱلۡغَيۡثَ وَيَعۡلَمُ مَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡحَامِۖ وَمَا تَدۡرِي نَفۡسࣱ مَّاذَا تَكۡسِبُ غَدࣰ اۖ وَمَا تَدۡرِي نَفۡسُۢ بِأَيِّ أَرۡضࣲ تَمُوتُۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرُۢ
31:34.en: Lo! Allah! With Him is knowledge of the Hour. He sendeth down the rain, and knoweth that which is in the wombs. No soul knoweth what it will earn to-morrow, and no soul knoweth in what land it will die. Lo! Allah is Knower, Aware

31:21.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ٱتَّبِعُواْ مَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ قَالُواْ بَلۡ نَتَّبِعُ مَا وَجَدۡنَا عَلَيۡهِ ءَابَآءَنَآۚ أَوَلَوۡ كَانَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ يَدۡعُوهُمۡ إِلَىٰ عَذَابِ ٱلسَّعِيرِ
31:21.en: And if it be said unto them: Follow that which Allah hath revealed, they say: Nay, but we follow that wherein we found our fathers. What! Even though the devil were inviting them unto the doom of flame

31:22.ar: ۞وَمَن يُسۡلِمۡ وَجۡهَهُۥٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحۡسِنࣱ فَقَدِ ٱسۡتَمۡسَكَ بِٱلۡعُرۡوَةِ ٱلۡوُثۡقَىٰۗ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلۡأُمُورِ
31:22.en: Whosoever surrendereth his purpose to Allah while doing good, he verily hath grasped the firm hand-hold. Unto Allah belongeth the sequel of all things

16:58.ar: وَإِذَا بُشِّرَ أَحَدُهُم بِٱلۡأُنثَىٰ ظَلَّ وَجۡهُهُۥ مُسۡوَدࣰّ ا وَهُوَ كَظِيمࣱ‏
16:58.en: When if one of them receiveth tidings of the birth of a female, his face remaineth darkened, and he is wroth inwardly

16:59.ar: يَتَوَٰرَىٰ مِنَ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ مِن سُوٓءِ مَا بُشِّرَ بِهِۦٓۚ أَيُمۡسِكُهُۥ عَلَىٰ هُونٍ أَمۡ يَدُسُّهُۥ فِي ٱلتُّرَابِۗ أَلَا سَآءَ مَا يَحۡكُمُونَ
16:59.en: He hideth himself from the folk because of the evil of that whereof he hath had tidings, (asking himself): Shall he keep it in contempt, or bury it beneath the dust. Verily evil is their judgment

7:171.ar: ۞وَإِذۡ نَتَقۡنَا ٱلۡجَبَلَ فَوۡقَهُمۡ كَأَنَّهُۥ ظُلَّةࣱ وَظَنُّوٓاْ أَنَّهُۥ وَاقِعُۢ بِهِمۡ خُذُواْ مَآ ءَاتَيۡنَٰكُم بِقُوَّةࣲ وَٱذۡكُرُواْ مَا فِيهِ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَتَّقُونَ
7:171.en: And when We shook the Mount above them as it were a covering, and they supposed that it was going to fall upon them (and We said): Hold fast that which We have given you, and remember that which is therein, that ye may ward off (evil)

53:26.ar: ۞وَكَم مِّن مَّلَكࣲ فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ لَا تُغۡنِي شَفَٰعَتُهُمۡ شَيۡـًٔا إِلَّا مِنۢ بَعۡدِ أَن يَأۡذَنَ ٱللَّهُ لِمَن يَشَآءُ وَيَرۡضَىٰٓ
53:26.en: And how many angels are in the heavens whose intercession availeth naught save after Allah giveth leave to whom He chooseth and accepteth

11:42.ar: وَهِيَ تَجۡرِي بِهِمۡ فِي مَوۡجࣲ كَٱلۡجِبَالِ وَنَادَىٰ نُوحٌ ٱبۡنَهُۥ وَكَانَ فِي مَعۡزِلࣲ يَٰبُنَيَّ ٱرۡكَب مَّعَنَا وَلَا تَكُن مَّعَ ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ
11:42.en: And it sailed with them amid waves like mountains, and Noah cried unto his son - and he was standing aloof - O my son! Come ride with us, and be not with the disbelievers

11:43.ar: قَالَ سَـَٔاوِيٓ إِلَىٰ جَبَلࣲ يَعۡصِمُنِي مِنَ ٱلۡمَآءِۚ قَالَ لَا عَاصِمَ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ مِنۡ أَمۡرِ ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا مَن رَّحِمَۚ وَحَالَ بَيۡنَهُمَا ٱلۡمَوۡجُ فَكَانَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُغۡرَقِينَ
11:43.en: He said: I shall betake me to some mountain that will save me from the water. (Noah) said: This day there is none that saveth from the commandment of Allah save him on whom He hath had mercy. And the wave came in between them, so he was among the drowned

11:44.ar: وَقِيلَ يَٰٓأَرۡضُ ٱبۡلَعِي مَآءَكِ وَيَٰسَمَآءُ أَقۡلِعِي وَغِيضَ ٱلۡمَآءُ وَقُضِيَ ٱلۡأَمۡرُ وَٱسۡتَوَتۡ عَلَى ٱلۡجُودِيِّۖ وَقِيلَ بُعۡدࣰ ا لِّلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
11:44.en: And it was said: O earth! Swallow thy water and, O sky! be cleared of clouds! And the water was made to subside. And the commandment was fulfilled. And it (the ship) came to rest upon (the mount) Al-Judi and it was said: A far removal for wrongdoing folk

11:45.ar: وَنَادَىٰ نُوحࣱ رَّبَّهُۥ فَقَالَ رَبِّ إِنَّ ٱبۡنِي مِنۡ أَهۡلِي وَإِنَّ وَعۡدَكَ ٱلۡحَقُّ وَأَنتَ أَحۡكَمُ ٱلۡحَٰكِمِينَ
11:45.en: And Noah cried unto his Lord and said: My Lord! Lo! my son is of my household! Surely Thy promise is the truth and Thou are the Most Just of Judges

11:46.ar: قَالَ يَٰنُوحُ إِنَّهُۥ لَيۡسَ مِنۡ أَهۡلِكَۖ إِنَّهُۥ عَمَلٌ غَيۡرُ صَٰلِحࣲۖ فَلَا تَسۡـَٔلۡنِ مَا لَيۡسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلۡمٌۖ إِنِّيٓ أَعِظُكَ أَن تَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِينَ
11:46.en: He said: O Noah! Lo! he is not of thy household; lo! he is of evil conduct, so ask not of Me that whereof thou hast no knowledge. I admonish thee lest thou be among the ignorant

52:21.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَٱتَّبَعَتۡهُمۡ ذُرِّيَّتُهُم بِإِيمَٰنٍ أَلۡحَقۡنَا بِهِمۡ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمۡ وَمَآ أَلَتۡنَٰهُم مِّنۡ عَمَلِهِم مِّن شَيۡءࣲۚ كُلُّ ٱمۡرِيِٕۭ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينࣱ‏
52:21.en: And they who believe and whose seed follow them in faith, We cause their seed to join them (there), and We deprive them of nought of their (life's) work. Every man is a pledge for that which he hath earned

sa0db2ODNmo.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman 29-34
sa0db2ODNmo.one_line: The closing verses of Luqman: Allah the All-Aware of intentions, patience and gratitude, and a Day when no parent avails a child.
sa0db2ODNmo.summary: Finishing Surat Luqman, he reads the closing page as Allah's commentary on Luqman's counsel. Healthy relations between generations need balance: neither the blind obedience of the old Arabs nor outright disobedience. The verses on night entering day and the sun and moon running to a set term are addressed to each individual: nothing lasts, young or old. Allah is al-Khabir, aware of the intentions behind deeds, and since no law can fix a corrupt intention, only fear of al-Haqq, al-Aliyy al-Kabir can. The ship image shows the two states of the believer, patience and gratitude, with gratitude the base and patience its placeholder, against the faithless ingrate who forgets his rescue. The call to all mankind to fear a Day when no parent avails a child and no child avails a parent means each is responsible for himself and serves the other only to save himself, and that neither generation replaces the other. Every generation repeats the same complaints about the next, but the Prophet never belittled the young and promoted them. The five keys of the unseen remind all that no one knows everything, so each should offer advice humbly, as Luqman did.

outline.heading: Recap: the pages that comment on Luqman's story
outline.gist: As in Al-Kahf, a central story is followed by verses that comment on it and draw attention to what we might have missed.

outline.heading: Balance between blind obedience and disobedience
outline.gist: The Quran did not come to reinforce ancestor worship but to correct it: benefit from elders, keep company with them kindly, and stay independent in belief.

outline.heading: Each generation acts for Allah, not as repayment
outline.gist: Elders raise and the young honour for Allah's sake, not as a transaction.

outline.heading: The Arabs who wanted sons for their own strength
outline.gist: Having children to gain protection and status led to despising daughters, the root of a chain of evils.

outline.heading: The pivotal verse: the firmest handhold
outline.gist: Submitting one's face to Allah alone, with ihsan, is the axis of these two pages and improves every relationship.

outline.heading: Recitation, and a note on two consecutive ha's
outline.gist: Reads verses 29 and 30 and notes that the two ha's are pronounced separately in this reading.

outline.heading: 'Do you not see' in the singular: an address to each person
outline.gist: Contrasted with the plural in verse 20, which called society to shared gratitude, this verse addresses each individual.

outline.heading: Night into day: nothing lasts
outline.gist: Whether old or young, do not deceive yourself that you are permanent.

outline.heading: Sun and moon to an appointed term; time itself ends
outline.gist: We understand time through day and night; prisoners deprived of them lose their minds; even this motion has a set end.

outline.heading: Al-Khabir: knowing what is in the chest
outline.gist: Distinguishes al-Alim, al-Sami, al-Basir, al-Latif and al-Khabir; al-Khabir knows intentions that leave no trace in the world of the senses.

outline.heading: No law can fix a corrupt intention
outline.gist: People can harm others without ever breaking a law; only Allah's knowledge of intentions reaches this, and He brings it out on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Allah is al-Haqq; what they call on besides Him is falsehood
outline.gist: Truth precedes justice; every word and act will be weighed on the scale of truth, and anything done for other than Him is void.

outline.heading: Relationships cannot be governed by rules alone
outline.gist: Institutions and laws can set conditions, but in marriage or any relationship a person with bad intention will find a way around them.

outline.heading: Al-Aliyy al-Kabir: names of majesty and warning
outline.gist: These names are used to warn; the human stands in awe before the One who is Truth and above all.

outline.heading: Recitation of the ship verses
outline.gist: Reads verses 31 and 32.

outline.heading: Two states: patience and gratitude
outline.gist: Gratitude is the default state; patience is the temporary substitute that keeps one under the umbrella of gratitude when harm makes thanks impossible.

outline.heading: Ships run by Allah's favour; waves like canopies
outline.gist: Had wood not floated humanity would never have spread; waves tower like mountains, as the mountain was raised over the Children of Israel.

outline.heading: Sincere in the storm
outline.gist: In terror, as when a plane drops, people repent and purify their intentions instantly; confess before death while it still helps.

outline.heading: 'Some of them are moderate': the promise half kept
outline.gist: Rescued, some trim their great sincerity, like one who vowed all his wealth and gave a little; look at yourself, not at those who forgot your favours.

outline.heading: Khattar and kafur: the opposite of sabbar and shakur
outline.gist: Khattar lacks patience and kafur lacks gratitude; kufr in its basic sense is the opposite of gratitude; ships, like having children, are a blessing with real risk.

outline.heading: Khattar: losing one's composure
outline.gist: The word appears only here: one who in hardship collapses and humiliates himself instead of holding firm.

outline.heading: Recitation of the closing verses
outline.gist: Reads verses 33 and 34.

outline.heading: 'O mankind, fear your Lord': the page as preparation
outline.gist: Addressed to all people because the generational problem exists in every society; the whole page introduced who your Lord is before commanding taqwa.

outline.heading: No parent avails a child, no child a parent
outline.gist: No one can step in for another on that Day; intercession happens only with Allah's permission.

outline.heading: Nuh and his son; righteous offspring joined to parents
outline.gist: Nuh's plea was refused because his son was not righteous, while believing descendants are raised to their parents' rank.

outline.heading: The Prophet tells his family to save themselves
outline.gist: Each is responsible for himself and does good to the other to save himself; the nominal sentence stresses that the child can never avail the parent.

outline.heading: Neither generation substitutes for the other
outline.gist: A second meaning of yajzi: one generation does not replace the other; every generation repeats the same tired complaints about the next.

outline.heading: The Prophet never belittled the young
outline.gist: He excused, forgave and promoted the young into leadership; deceptive worldly life and Shaytan make people think otherwise.

outline.heading: The five keys of the unseen: no one knows everything
outline.gist: Conflict is over who knows more; only Allah knows the Hour, the rain, the womb, tomorrow and where one dies, so all should be humble.

outline.heading: Back to Luqman's gentle counsel
outline.gist: Luqman advised with love and even humour, without wanting control over his son.

outline.heading: Reread Luqman after the commentary
outline.gist: Returning to Luqman's words after Allah's commentary reveals more depth.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Youth, their challenges and their role

No law can control intentions

contemporary: Prison practices in wars and under regimes in Muslim lands
Generational complaints about youth glued to their phones
takeaways: Check your intentions, since Allah knows what no law can reach
Stay in a state of gratitude, and be patient when gratitude is not possible
Remember your rescue in hardship and keep the promises you made then
Do your duty to parents and children for Allah, knowing each answers for himself
Stop belittling the younger generation; excuse and empower them as the Prophet did

31:21.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ٱتَّبِعُواْ مَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ قَالُواْ بَلۡ نَتَّبِعُ مَا وَجَدۡنَا عَلَيۡهِ ءَابَآءَنَآۚ أَوَلَوۡ كَانَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ يَدۡعُوهُمۡ إِلَىٰ عَذَابِ ٱلسَّعِيرِ
31:21.en: And if it be said unto them: Follow that which Allah hath revealed, they say: Nay, but we follow that wherein we found our fathers. What! Even though the devil were inviting them unto the doom of flame

31:22.ar: ۞وَمَن يُسۡلِمۡ وَجۡهَهُۥٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحۡسِنࣱ فَقَدِ ٱسۡتَمۡسَكَ بِٱلۡعُرۡوَةِ ٱلۡوُثۡقَىٰۗ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلۡأُمُورِ
31:22.en: Whosoever surrendereth his purpose to Allah while doing good, he verily hath grasped the firm hand-hold. Unto Allah belongeth the sequel of all things

31:23.ar: وَمَن كَفَرَ فَلَا يَحۡزُنكَ كُفۡرُهُۥٓۚ إِلَيۡنَا مَرۡجِعُهُمۡ فَنُنَبِّئُهُم بِمَا عَمِلُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمُۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ
31:23.en: And whosoever disbelieveth, let not his disbelief afflict thee (O Muhammad). Unto Us is their return, and We shall tell them what they did. Lo! Allah is Aware of what is in the breasts (of men)

31:24.ar: نُمَتِّعُهُمۡ قَلِيلࣰ ا ثُمَّ نَضۡطَرُّهُمۡ إِلَىٰ عَذَابٍ غَلِيظࣲ‏
31:24.en: We give them comfort for a little, and then We drive them to a heavy doom

31:25.ar: وَلَئِن سَأَلۡتَهُم مَّنۡ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ ٱللَّهُۚ قُلِ ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِۚ بَلۡ أَكۡثَرُهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
31:25.en: If thou shouldst ask them: Who created the heavens and the earth? they would answer: Allah. Say: Praise be to Allah! But most of them know not

31:26.ar: لِلَّهِ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلۡغَنِيُّ ٱلۡحَمِيدُ
31:26.en: Unto Allah belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth. Lo! Allah, He is the Absolute, the Owner of Praise

31:27.ar: وَلَوۡ أَنَّمَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ مِن شَجَرَةٍ أَقۡلَٰمࣱ وَٱلۡبَحۡرُ يَمُدُّهُۥ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦ سَبۡعَةُ أَبۡحُرࣲ مَّا نَفِدَتۡ كَلِمَٰتُ ٱللَّهِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمࣱ‏
31:27.en: And if all the trees in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to help it, (were ink), the words of Allah could not be exhausted. Lo! Allah is Mighty, Wise

31:28.ar: مَّا خَلۡقُكُمۡ وَلَا بَعۡثُكُمۡ إِلَّا كَنَفۡسࣲ وَٰحِدَةٍۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ سَمِيعُۢ بَصِيرٌ
31:28.en: Your creation and your raising (from the dead) are only as (the creation and the raising of) a single soul. Lo! Allah is Hearer, Knower

31:14.ar: وَوَصَّيۡنَا ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ بِوَٰلِدَيۡهِ حَمَلَتۡهُ أُمُّهُۥ وَهۡنًا عَلَىٰ وَهۡنࣲ وَفِصَٰلُهُۥ فِي عَامَيۡنِ أَنِ ٱشۡكُرۡ لِي وَلِوَٰلِدَيۡكَ إِلَيَّ ٱلۡمَصِيرُ
31:14.en: And We have enjoined upon man concerning his partners - His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years - Give thanks unto Me and unto thy parents. Unto Me is the journeying

31:15.ar: وَإِن جَٰهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تُشۡرِكَ بِي مَا لَيۡسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلۡمࣱ فَلَا تُطِعۡهُمَاۖ وَصَاحِبۡهُمَا فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَا مَعۡرُوفࣰ اۖ وَٱتَّبِعۡ سَبِيلَ مَنۡ أَنَابَ إِلَيَّۚ ثُمَّ إِلَيَّ مَرۡجِعُكُمۡ فَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
31:15.en: But if they strive with thee to make thee ascribe unto Me as partner that of which thou hast no knowledge, then obey them not. Consort with them in the world kindly, and follow the path of him who repenteth unto Me. Then unto Me will be your return, and I shall tell you what ye used to do

23:68.ar: أَفَلَمۡ يَدَّبَّرُواْ ٱلۡقَوۡلَ أَمۡ جَآءَهُم مَّا لَمۡ يَأۡتِ ءَابَآءَهُمُ ٱلۡأَوَّلِينَ
23:68.en: Have they not pondered the Word, or hath that come unto them which came not unto their fathers of old

18:109.ar: قُل لَّوۡ كَانَ ٱلۡبَحۡرُ مِدَادࣰ ا لِّكَلِمَٰتِ رَبِّي لَنَفِدَ ٱلۡبَحۡرُ قَبۡلَ أَن تَنفَدَ كَلِمَٰتُ رَبِّي وَلَوۡ جِئۡنَا بِمِثۡلِهِۦ مَدَدࣰ ا
18:109.en: Say: Though the sea became ink for the Words of my Lord, verily the sea would be used up before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even though We brought the like thereof to help

4:94.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا ضَرَبۡتُمۡ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَتَبَيَّنُواْ وَلَا تَقُولُواْ لِمَنۡ أَلۡقَىٰٓ إِلَيۡكُمُ ٱلسَّلَٰمَ لَسۡتَ مُؤۡمِنࣰ ا تَبۡتَغُونَ عَرَضَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا فَعِندَ ٱللَّهِ مَغَانِمُ كَثِيرَةࣱۚ كَذَٰلِكَ كُنتُم مِّن قَبۡلُ فَمَنَّ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ فَتَبَيَّنُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ خَبِيرࣰ ا
4:94.en: O ye who believe! When ye go forth (to fight) in the way of Allah, be careful to discriminate, and say not unto one who offereth you peace: "Thou art not a believer," seeking the chance profits of this life (so that ye may despoil him). With Allah are plenteous spoils. Even thus (as he now is) were ye before; but Allah hath since then been gracious unto you. Therefore take care to discriminate. Allah is ever Informed of what ye do

BEg5c_q5A-8.speaker: adnan
BEg5c_q5A-8.speaker_note: Sunday Arabic tafsir series on Surat Luqman in his usual voice; refers to his own children and life in Canada
BEg5c_q5A-8.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman 21-28
BEg5c_q5A-8.one_line: Luqman 21-28: no blind following of fathers, submitting only to Allah, and how magnifying Allah heals the relationship between parents and children.
BEg5c_q5A-8.summary: Picking up after Luqman's counsel to his son, he stresses that the passage does not demand blind following of the older generation. The Quran mocks those who reject truth only because their fathers did not know it, and even long-dead scholars are not followed without discussion. Only Allah is followed unconditionally, and one reaches that through long reflection, with ihsan as the firmest handhold. The verses that follow (25-28) on Allah's creation, self-sufficiency and endless words are placed there to persuade the believer why He alone deserves submission. He then applies this to families: when parents raise children for their own entitlement, or children serve parents only to repay a debt, love dies and estrangement follows. Both must do it for Allah. Parents do not own their children's career or home choices and must not wield Allah's anger as a weapon. Since no one has exhausted Allah's wisdom, elders should share what they know humbly, and since humanity is like one soul, a father should remember he was once the same rebellious son, break inherited harmful patterns, and be patient as the Prophet was. He closes by asking elders to show tenderness to the young or face empty mosques.

outline.heading: Recap: Luqman's counsel and the pages that comment on it
outline.gist: Situates the two pages after Luqman's advice as commentary on its principles.

outline.heading: Not blind following of fathers
outline.gist: Luqman's advice is to be heard and weighed, not followed blindly. The Jahiliyyah had real virtues and real vices; the Quran asks people to keep the good and drop the bad.

outline.heading: Submitting one's face to Allah alone
outline.gist: Only Allah's word is accepted without debate, and one arrives there only after long reflection on the universe, history and revelation.

outline.heading: Not even scholars are followed unconditionally
outline.gist: A problem in the ummah is treating a dead scholar's view as final; ideas should be discussed with living scholars.

outline.heading: Ihsan and the firmest handhold
outline.gist: Ihsan means acting with pure motive and the best method, free of ego and control; with it one holds the handhold that never breaks.

outline.heading: The verse as the basis between generations
outline.gist: Life is one generation leaving and another arriving; when both submit to Allah the relationship is sound, when each has its own agenda it breaks.

outline.heading: Recitation of the new passage
outline.gist: Reads verses 25 to 28 aloud.

outline.heading: Nafidat with dal, not dhal
outline.gist: A recitation point: nafad (to run out) versus nafadh (to penetrate) changes the meaning, as in the end of Al-Kahf; why the tongue slips toward dhal.

outline.heading: Why these verses follow Luqman's advice
outline.gist: Wherever the Quran commands reliance and submission it follows with verses about Allah, as if persuading you why He alone deserves it.

outline.heading: Everyone admits a creator; they differ on His attributes
outline.gist: Even Quraysh and most modern atheists accept a great originating force; the disagreement is over His description, which Allah supplies Himself.

outline.heading: Magnifying Allah is behind every healthy relationship
outline.gist: Whoever does not magnify Allah magnifies his own ego, which makes relationships between people and generations impossible.

outline.heading: Idols as a loophole from morality; praise in Luqman
outline.gist: Idols, soothsayers and lenient clerics let people escape full moral commitment; notes the recurring theme of praise and gratitude in the surah.

outline.heading: Al-Ghani al-Hamid: your obedience adds nothing to Him
outline.gist: Allah needs no one; submission benefits only the servant, which is why one should turn to no one else.

outline.heading: Parents who raise children for entitlement
outline.gist: Raising children not for Allah breeds a sense of being owed, which drives love out of the child's heart even if he still obeys.

outline.heading: Ibn Umar and the man who carried his mother through Hajj
outline.gist: Carrying her did not repay one breath of labour, because she bore him wishing him life while he bore her wishing her rest.

outline.heading: Children must honour parents for Allah
outline.gist: Service done only to repay a debt runs dry; children see their parents' faults clearly, and where criticising parents is permitted it shows what they really feel.

outline.heading: Siblings who compete to serve parents
outline.gist: Those who see parents as a door to Paradise compete to care for them; quotes his late teacher that the elderly need tender people around them; the Prophet told Fatimah he could not save her from Allah.

outline.heading: Children as a gift; the cost of removing Allah from the equation
outline.gist: Without Allah in the relationship estrangement and curses follow; the verses on parents in this surah come directly from Allah, setting limits on obeying them.

outline.heading: What parents' rights are and are not
outline.gist: Parents may command good and forbid wrong but may not choose a child's career or home, nor use their anger as Allah's weapon.

outline.heading: Raising children for Allah, not to serve you
outline.gist: Addresses new fathers: a compassionate society needs a right foundation; you did not bring a child into the world to be your servant.

outline.heading: Self-interest in having children; how the righteous read these verses
outline.gist: A child raised for your benefit owes you little love; the early generations recited these verses with lowered heads.

outline.heading: 'Most of them do not know': surface versus deep knowledge
outline.gist: Knowing Allah is Creator is shallow knowledge unless one builds obedience and submission on it.

outline.heading: All trees as pens, seven seas as ink
outline.gist: Al-Hamid is praiseworthy in every state; even with every tree as a pen and the oceans sevenfold as ink Allah's words would not run out.

outline.heading: Elders do not know everything: share with humility
outline.gist: Since Allah's wisdom never runs out, the older generation should offer its little extra knowledge humbly rather than claim to know it all.

outline.heading: Al-Aziz al-Hakim: every command serves you
outline.gist: His essence is beyond grasp, and every command carries benefit in this life before the next, so complaining about prohibitions is foolish.

outline.heading: Created and raised as one soul: rewind the film
outline.gist: Two readings of the verse; the angry father was himself the son his father was angry with, now visible for the first time through childhood videos.

outline.heading: Your child is like you: be patient as others were with you
outline.gist: The child inherited your traits; if your father was harsh, do not repeat it.

outline.heading: Breaking the chains of inherited faults
outline.gist: Neither rejecting everything nor accepting everything from parents; take the good, leave the bad, so each generation is better.

outline.heading: The Prophet broke the habits of Jahiliyyah
outline.gist: Anas reports he never struck anyone or asked why something was or was not done; this is ihsan in its purest form.

outline.heading: Hunayn: 'You want evil for yourself and I want good for you'
outline.gist: A man who intended treachery was met with the Prophet's wish for his guidance.

outline.heading: 'So were you before': no hasty judgments of the young
outline.gist: Even in battle the Quran says verify and remember you were once the same; elders forget their own mistakes and become harsh.

outline.heading: Elders must be tender or mosques empty
outline.gist: Respect from the young and compassion from the old must go together or the mosques die with the older generation.

outline.heading: Outro

W7xfEZbvErI.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: The Good News
W7xfEZbvErI.one_line: Closes the character series: the Quran exposes human flaws and gives the good news that insight makes change possible, as the Prophet's life proves.
W7xfEZbvErI.summary: Closing his series, he states its thesis: a central purpose of the Quran was to make the human being understand himself, naming openly the greed, selfishness, haste, panic and vanity built into the human psyche, and then showing what he can become. Honest self-examination confirms it, and the Quran does not want these traits masked or denied. The good news is insight: unlike animals and small children, the human can see his own traits, which is why Al-Qiyamah describes a self-reproaching soul and a man who is a witness against himself however many excuses he offers. Insight without the ability to change would be a cruel joke; the whole point of the Quran is that you can hit the brakes. Vice feels good for a moment and leaves emptiness and shame; virtue feels good long term. Pretending to have no flaws fools nobody, least of all Allah; the shame lies in not changing what you could. The Quran speaks in scenarios of hardship, success, harm and praise, and the Prophet, whose character was the Quran, proves it works: forty years of losses, persecution and war, yet he entered Mecca bowed over his mount, praising Allah and seeking forgiveness as An-Nasr instructed. If you do not understand why, go back and read the book.

outline.heading: Opening
The Quran came to help man understand himself
outline.gist: As it was revealed to the Prophet and the companions, the Quran made clear that a main purpose was to show the human how he instinctively behaves, every shortcoming of the human psyche, and what he can become.

outline.heading: Do not mask your flaws
outline.gist: That is uplifting: honest self-examination shows each of us negative urges, thoughts and feelings, and an unimpressive morality we learn to mask and ignore. The Quran wants the opposite: embrace who you are, do not hide it, because Allah Himself exposes openly that this is how the human is.

outline.heading: The good news is insight
outline.gist: The same traits let humans survive and conquer the earth, but since Adam they must no longer define us. Animals and small children act on instinct and lack insight, so we do not hold them accountable; you and I have it.

outline.heading: Al-Qiyamah: he wants to sin guilt-free
outline.gist: By the Day of Judgment and by the self-reproaching soul: man thinks his bones will not be gathered, but he will be restored to his fingertips. What he really wants is an excuse to follow his desires guilt-free, so he asks mockingly when this Day is.

outline.heading: No refuge on that Day
outline.gist: Sight is dazzled, the moon eclipsed, sun and moon joined as the cosmos collapses; man asks where to flee, but there is no refuge, and to your Lord is the destination.

outline.heading: A witness against himself
outline.gist: Man will be informed of all he sent forward and held back, yet it is not news to him: he always knew, and his excuses change nothing. He may have fooled his family, the court and all humanity and won applause, but he knew and so did Allah.

outline.heading: You can be defined by the opposite
outline.gist: Insight is the good news because you can change: you can be empathetic, loving, careful, resilient, patient, wise, selfless and generous, and living that way feels good long term.

outline.heading: Vice feels good for a moment
outline.gist: Greed and selfishness feel good only at the moment you get what you wanted; then come emptiness and a bad mood you cannot explain, shame that you could have been better, and distraction so you do not have to face the mirror.

outline.heading: Insight without change would be a cruel joke
outline.gist: That is why Allah speaks of people changing what is in themselves, the verse everyone quotes: you have the capacity. Insight with no power to change would be a nightmare, watching yourself and humanity march inevitably to destruction; a lion that kills another's cubs has no insight and cannot change.

outline.heading: Hit the brakes: embrace your nature, then control it
outline.gist: The whole point of the Quran is that you can stop and turn around. You were created selfish, hasty and panicky: embrace it but control it, so that it does not rule you and you can be calm, patient and composed.

outline.heading: His character was the Quran
outline.gist: Asked about his character, Aisha said it was the Quran: he lived the changes it described, and those around him transformed themselves in a mesmerizing way. It was not miraculous; they opened the book and listened.

outline.heading: Interlude
Who are you fooling? Allah says you are
outline.gist: Claiming not to be arrogant, selfish or panicky fools no one; Allah says we are, so every one of us is vain. There is no shame in being created so; the shame is having insight and the ability to replace it with humility, empathy and selflessness, and not doing it.

outline.heading: You cannot change what you will not admit
outline.gist: The Quran has no interest in the charade. First admit that you panic when things go wrong, sink when you do not get what you want, and want to gloat when you do; the question is why, with insight, you did not change it. The companions wore no facades.

outline.heading: A potential that comes from Allah
outline.gist: The Quran also says there is more to us: a beautiful potential from Allah, what was blown into us, capable of wanting more and taming the rest. Embrace your nature without shaming yourself or others, then decide what must change.

outline.heading: The Quran talks in scenarios
outline.gist: When hardship or goodness comes, when you get or miss what you want, when people harm or praise you, when you fail or succeed: here is your life, here is how you will want to feel, here is how you should behave.

outline.heading: Forty years of blows
outline.gist: Read his life that way: he lost his father, mother and grandfather, grew up unnoticed in a crowded house, worked honestly without wealth or status while worse people led, and lost both his sons.

outline.heading: Prophecy brought slander, persecution and war
outline.gist: Then the one reputation he had, honesty, was tarnished: liar, sorcerer, traitor. Years of abuse of him, his family and followers; his wife, uncles, daughters and cousins died; he was expelled and forced, though no man of war, into wars meant to annihilate him.

outline.heading: Mecca surrenders
outline.gist: Through it all he kept empathy, reasonableness and his ground. After years of loss, poverty and exile he walked into Mecca at the head of an army, and those who had expelled him and tried to murder him surrendered completely.

outline.heading: An-Nasr: what to do at the top of the mountain
outline.gist: When victory comes and people enter Islam in crowds, now out of your strength more than conviction, glorify your Lord and seek forgiveness. He was always seeking forgiveness; at the top of the mountain, that is what you do.

outline.heading: He entered Mecca bowed flat
outline.gist: He entered Mecca with his face pressed to his mount's mane, lying flat in humility before Allah, not chest out as the conquering son returned. If you do not know why, go back to the book he shared; otherwise what is the point of learning his life?

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Relationship with the Quran: reading, reflecting, living it
themes.note: A main purpose of the Quran was to help the human understand himself, exposing his instinctive flaws and pointing to what he can become; this is what transformed the Prophet and the companions.

themes.label: Self-honesty and self-accountability (muhasabah)
themes.note: The good news is insight: humans, unlike animals, can see their own greed and selfishness, which is why they are accountable. On the Day the human will be a witness against himself even if he fooled everyone around him.

themes.label: Accountability before Allah and goals
themes.note: Al-Qiyamah: the human wants an excuse to follow his desires guilt-free and mocks the Day, but there will be no refuge and he will be informed of everything he did and held back.

themes.label: Character and manners (akhlaq)
themes.note: You can be defined by the opposite traits: empathy, patience, wisdom, generosity. Virtue feels good long term; greed and selfishness feel good for a moment and leave emptiness, a bad mood and shame you cover with distraction.

themes.label: Tazkiyah: purifying and training the self
themes.note: Insight without the ability to change would be a cruel joke; the Quran's whole point is that you can hit the brakes. Embrace your selfish, hasty, panicky nature, then control it so it does not rule you.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: Aisha's answer that his character was the Quran: he lived the changes the Quran described, and the companions' transformation came from just listening to the book.

themes.label: Self-honesty and self-accountability (muhasabah)
themes.note: Acting as if you are not vain or selfish is a lie the Quran has no interest in; you cannot change what you will not admit. The shame is not having the trait but not changing it when you could. The companions wore no facades.

themes.label: Relationship with the Quran: reading, reflecting, living it
themes.note: The Quran talks in scenarios: when hardship or ease comes, when you get or lose what you want, when people harm or praise you. It tells you how you will feel and how you should behave.

themes.label: Seerah events and their lessons
themes.note: The Prophet's life as forty years of blows, then slander, persecution, bereavement, exile and war, ending in the conquest of Mecca; through it all he kept empathy and composure.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: An-Nasr told him that at the moment of victory he should praise Allah and seek forgiveness. He entered Mecca lying flat over his mount, head down, not as a gloating conqueror; that is what you do at the top of your mountain.

quran.point: Oath by the Day of Judgment and by the soul that holds itself accountable: the human has insight.
Man doubts his bones can be gathered; Allah will restore him to the fingerprint. He really just wants to keep sinning guilt-free and asks when this Day is.
Dazzled sight, eclipsed moon, sun and moon joined; man asks where to flee; no refuge; to your Lord is the destination.
Man will be told what he sent forward and held back, yet he is a witness against himself however many excuses he offers; he always knew.
Allah does not change a people's condition until they change what is in themselves: the verse everyone quotes, revealed because humans have the capacity to change.
When victory comes and people enter Islam in droves, glorify your Lord and seek forgiveness: the instruction for the top of the mountain.

hadith.gist: Aisha, asked about the Prophet's character, answered that his character was the Quran.

maxims: Embrace your nature, but change it
Control it so it does not rule you
The shame is not having the problem but not changing it
You have insight; animals do not
The Quran talks in scenarios
On top of the mountain, praise Him and seek forgiveness

stories.who: The Prophet's forty years of losses and the years of persecution
stories.point: Orphaned, overlooked, poor, bereaved of both sons, slandered, abused, exiled and forced into wars, he kept empathy and reasonableness; the Quran's teaching made that possible.

stories.who: The conquest of Mecca
stories.point: After being expelled and hunted, he returned at the head of an army Mecca could not resist, yet entered bowed over his mount, praising Allah and seeking forgiveness as An-Nasr commanded.

takeaways: Admit your instinctive flaws (vanity, selfishness, haste, panic) openly instead of pretending they are not there; you cannot change what you deny.
Use your insight: when you catch a trait you know is wrong, actively control it rather than mask it or distract yourself.
Read the Quran as scenarios for your own life, noting how it tells you to feel and act in hardship, success, harm and praise.
Study the Prophet's life as proof that the Quran's transformation is achievable, not miraculous.
When Allah grants you success, respond with praise and seeking forgiveness rather than gloating.

S_ZE7WEC_UM.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Muddaththir, Part 6: Verses 42-56
S_ZE7WEC_UM.one_line: The four answers from the people of Saqar, especially neglecting the needy and going with the flow, and why denying accountability is the real root.
S_ZE7WEC_UM.summary: He opens with a test for any way of life: if everyone lived by your values, would the world still work? Islam passes that test, and the seven commands of Al-Muddaththir are behaviours that make it work, supported by three core pieces: accepting truth, keeping the big picture and believing in accountability. The closing verses let us hear, from inside the Fire, why people ended up there: they did not pray, did not feed the needy, went along with whatever others did, and denied the Day until death came. He finds these among the most frightening verses because the two middle answers are rarely preached; he stresses that taking principled stands and caring for the vulnerable are part of salvation, and that the herd mentality, plus Muslims' neglect of history, never protects anyone. Intercession helps only with Allah's permission. People fled the Prophet's reminder like startled wild donkeys from a lion, each wanting his own revelation, but a double 'bal' reveals the true root: they did not fear the Hereafter. He asks everyone to check whether they are fully certain of accountability, and stresses that the Quran is a reminder, not coercion.

outline.heading: What Islam gives you and what it asks you to carry to the world
outline.gist: Al-Muzzammil covers what you draw from Islam inwardly, Al-Muddaththir the ethical standard and behaviours you offer the world, because Islam is not only for personal gain.

outline.heading: The test of any way of life: would the world work if everyone lived it?
outline.gist: Values are sound only if everyone could live by them; greed fails because the world collapses if all are greedy, while the surah's seven commands, giving without reminding of favours, purity of soul and clothes, just stands and meaningful da'wah, pass.

outline.heading: First core piece recalled: accept the truth even after long error
outline.gist: The commands only work if you accept truth when you see it, unlike Walid, who saw it but built a narrative to tarnish the Prophet rather than admit he was wrong.

outline.heading: Second core piece recalled: do not get lost in details
outline.gist: Every picture needs details, but questioning why an angle is 90 and not 80 loses what matters, and in Islam that obsession harms more than it benefits.

outline.heading: Third core piece recalled: without accountability the whole philosophy collapses
outline.gist: Every soul is held by its deeds except the people of the right, who never saw deeds as payment and sought only Allah's mercy; without belief in accountability Islam falls apart.

outline.heading: Interlude
In the gardens they ask about the criminals, and the answers come from inside the Fire
outline.gist: The people of Paradise ask after old friends and are shown where they are; scholars debate the most hopeful verse, but he finds these the most fearful because the answers come from the throats of people in Jahannam.

outline.heading: Recitation of the closing passage
outline.gist: He recites from verse 42 to the end of the surah and remarks that even an untrained ear senses its linguistic and rhythmic mastery.

outline.heading: 'What led you into Saqar?' Four answers straight from the Fire
outline.gist: Shown their friends, the people of Paradise ask what forced them into the burning Fire, since no one goes there willingly; the four answers need no other witness.

outline.heading: 'We were not of those who prayed': refusing Allah's offer to speak with Him
outline.gist: Salah is Allah's offer of a meeting and conversation; they shrugged it off as worthless.

outline.heading: The first and last answers are accepted; the middle two are the struggle
outline.gist: Every Muslim agrees that not praying and denying the Day lead to ruin, and the last mirrors the surah's third core piece, but many wish the two middle answers were not there.

outline.heading: 'We did not feed the needy'
outline.gist: Most people sweat for their wealth and never think of giving it away unless it brings recognition; the miskin is anyone who cannot manage and needs someone to support and champion them.

outline.heading: 'We plunged in with those who plunged': going with the flow
outline.gist: Khawd here means talking and doing whatever is meaningless because everyone else does; the first, second and fourth answers seem fair, but this one is striking to hear from inside the Fire.

outline.heading: Rising to warn means taking a stand: hiding in the herd is a rookie move
outline.gist: The surah's opening command means take a stand and live by principle; dancing when they dance and keeping your head among the heads never protects you from catastrophe, oppression or loss.

outline.heading: Muslims have lost touch with history
outline.gist: As an ummah we no longer study the flow of civilisations, so we keep repeating the mistakes of others and of our ancestors, including drifting with the tide because it is easier.

outline.heading: Settle yourselves firmly: the Prophet's warning against being a yes-man
outline.gist: The Prophet warned against the imma'ah who bends with whatever people do and told us to plant our feet like a home, a watan; the people of the Fire stood for nothing and joined in alcohol and zina because everyone did.

outline.heading: 'We denied the Day of Judgment until certainty came'
outline.gist: He recaps the four voices; you can claim belief in accountability and still end up here if none of your choices show fear of being asked, and certainty here means death.

outline.heading: No intercession helps them except by Allah's permission
outline.gist: After recapping the seven commands and three core pieces, he explains that no intercessor, not even the angels or the Prophet, can help except after Allah grants permission and accepts it.

outline.heading: The sandwich: the middle answers are rarely preached
outline.gist: Muslims accept the outer answers, prayer and belief in the Day, but feeding the needy and taking meaningful stands are rarely talked about, though the people of the Fire name them.

outline.heading: Allah's words in one of the earliest surahs: the herd mentality leads to the Fire
outline.gist: If he said this on his own no one would accept it, but it comes in perhaps the third or fourth surah revealed: going with the crowd feels safe, while objecting to oppression is unpopular and scary, yet only the stand serves you in the Hereafter.

outline.heading: Why do they turn away from the reminder?
outline.gist: Allah asks the Prophet what is wrong with people who turn from a simple reminder; narrations describe Meccans scattering in different directions when he approached.

outline.heading: Like startled wild donkeys fleeing a lion
outline.gist: Wild donkeys flee a lion or hunter, qaswarah, because this life is all they have; the people fled the one who came to save them.

outline.heading: Each wants pages of revelation of his own
outline.gist: Bal dismisses fear as the reason: each wants spread-out pages addressed to him personally, not content with the Prophet as the vessel, out of arrogance and an inflated ego.

outline.heading: Could revelation work that way for everyone?
outline.gist: Apply the opening test: if each person demanded his own angel and his own Quran we would all be prophets; anyone who thinks himself the exception fails it.

outline.heading: Two 'bal' in a row: the rarest correction
outline.gist: Bal denies the previous point and affirms a new one; two in a row is the only case he knows in the Quran, peeling back fear and then entitlement to reach the real reason.

outline.heading: 'Nay, they do not fear the Hereafter': the root beneath every excuse
outline.gist: The underlying problem is that they do not believe they will be held accountable; when Allah digs two levels deep it applies to all of us, so a lack of commitment often means you do not truly believe.

outline.heading: Interlude
Ask yourself whether you are 100% certain of accountability
outline.gist: Whenever he speaks about death his audience halves, because ignoring it is easier; anything short of a full yes means the philosophy of Islam will not hold for you.

outline.heading: The Arabs revered God more than distorted scriptures portray Him
outline.gist: The Arabs did not deny Allah and held Him in reverence, unlike the vengeful portrayal in today's altered Torah and Bible; they only added associates to make things easier.

outline.heading: Their real denial: resurrection and the reckoning
outline.gist: They held that we live until time takes us; the Prophet's two uphill battles were removing associates and establishing that we will return and read back the book we authored.

outline.heading: 'Nay, it is a reminder': no coercion
outline.gist: Everything heard is a reminder offered with no intention of force; take it or leave it.

outline.heading: Communities present reminders; they do not force behaviour
outline.gist: Communities are not accountable for forcibly changing people; their job is to present reminders in ways people can understand and relate to.

outline.heading: Whoever wills will take heed: don't end up on the wrong side of the dialogue
outline.gist: Wrong choices may place you on the wrong side of the conversation you just heard; whoever intends to will benefit from the reminder.

outline.heading: None remember except as Allah wills
outline.gist: You are not forced against your will, yet nothing happens against His will either; that keeps the relationship clear.

outline.heading: He is worthy of taqwa and of forgiveness
outline.gist: He alone deserves that you protect yourself from His punishment and seek His forgiveness; another reading, which he prefers for the flow, is that He alone can grant protection and forgiveness.

outline.heading: Outro

ZydqE-N_xZA.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Mortality, Episode 22
ZydqE-N_xZA.one_line: Opening the pillar of accepting mortality and accountability: why nothing in the deen works without it, Adam's fear of death, and how to accept it.
ZydqE-N_xZA.summary: The sheikh begins the second of his five pillars of tazkiyah: accepting mortality and accountability to Allah. He warns it is the topic that thins the crowd, yet without it the whole ethical argument of Islam collapses, since being good only makes sense to the privileged unless there is death and judgment. A third of the Quran deals with it, and the companions were so convinced that the Prophet had to restrain them. He separates death, an unknown moment not worth obsessing over and never to be celebrated, from mortality, the fact that you will end, which must be accepted and not merely known. Adam had everything, yet Shaytan reached him only through the fear of death, offering the tree of immortality; that fear drove the first act of disobedience. Adam later gave Dawud forty of his years and nearly asked for them back. Imagining immortality shows that time would lose all value. Earlier generations met death often; modern people meet it late and exempt themselves, as drivers do from traffic rules. He asks listeners to contemplate their mortality carefully, with a mental-health caution, and points to the calm deaths of the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Bilal, his oncology patients, and the hadith on weakness from fear of death.

outline.gist: Being good is easy to argue when a system benefits you; for those on the losing side, morality without judgment has no basis.

outline.gist: Take mortality, then accountability, out of the deen and no argument survives.

outline.heading: Death is a moment; do not obsess over it
outline.gist: Death is an unknown point in time that will always come too early; planning for or fearing that moment is pointless.

outline.heading: We never celebrate death; we accept mortality
outline.gist: Even a martyr's death is a calamity; what must be accepted is that you will end.

outline.heading: Knowing is not accepting
outline.gist: Knowing you will die differs greatly from accepting it, which the coming weeks will show.

outline.heading: Adam had everything
outline.gist: Companionship, safety, food, beauty and closeness to Allah, with one tree forbidden.

outline.heading: The tree of immortality
outline.gist: It was not curiosity about the forbidden; Shaytan offered him eternal life.

outline.heading: The deal of life ends in death
outline.gist: Like a young adult told the whole plan of life, Adam liked everything except that he was a servant and would die.

outline.heading: Fear of death caused the first sin
outline.gist: Shaytan tried pitch after pitch until immortality made Adam flinch, then swore he was a sincere adviser.

outline.heading: A lifetime learning to accept
outline.gist: Adam spent the rest of his life accepting mortality; Allah showed him his descendants as points of light.

outline.heading: Adam's only question about Dawud
outline.gist: He asked only how long Dawud would live, as parents ache knowing their children will die.

outline.heading: Forty years given and almost taken back
outline.gist: When the angel came, Adam nearly asked for the years back; life's basic beauty makes losing it hard.

outline.heading: If you lived forever, time would be worthless
outline.gist: Time is the one capital you can never buy back; without an end, nothing would ever be done today.

outline.heading: Accept it, do not celebrate it
outline.gist: Not enjoying or welcoming mortality, but being at peace that it can come at any moment, which takes steps.

outline.heading: Earlier generations lived alongside death
outline.gist: With a median lifespan around 38, war and no antibiotics, the companions saw death often; modern medicine made it a stranger.

outline.heading: Death is enough as a reminder
outline.gist: Remembering death needed little prompting in their time, so the Prophet's advice was simply to remember it.

outline.heading: We meet death late in life
outline.gist: In the West most people have no experience of death until late and are never taught about it when young.

outline.heading: The human gift of self-exemption
outline.gist: Rules apply to everyone but slightly less to me, as on the road or in a queue; we do the same with death.

outline.heading: Contemplate your own mortality
outline.gist: This week, think about what your end would look and feel like.

outline.heading: A caution for those who are struggling
outline.gist: Anyone struggling with mental health or a reason to live should be careful and discuss this with their therapist.

outline.heading: Near-death experiences wear off
outline.gist: People change after a brush with death, then slide back within years because mortality was never truly accepted.

outline.heading: A good ending is what counts
outline.gist: The Prophet kept asking for a good end; marriages and tournaments are remembered by how they end.

outline.heading: How the Prophet and companions died
outline.gist: The Prophet chose the highest companion; Abu Bakr corrected Aisha's poetry, Umar asked for his face on the ground, Uthman refused bloodshed, Bilal smiled to meet his loved ones.

outline.heading: Death is hard for everyone
outline.gist: The stupor of death comes to all; preparation changes how it is met.

outline.heading: Conversations about mortality in oncology
outline.gist: Many of his clinic visits are, in effect, conversations about death coming sooner than hoped, and people respond according to how they lived.

outline.heading: The dying scholar and his grandsons
outline.gist: Prompted to say la ilaha illa Allah, he told them it was mixed in his blood and to go learn it themselves.

outline.heading: The 92-year-old who wanted two more years
outline.gist: Asked what he hoped for, a gravely ill patient wanted two more years, and then two more: death is never far enough away.

outline.heading: A different way to live
outline.gist: Accepting mortality and accountability gave the companions a different view of life, as near-death survivors sometimes gain.

outline.heading: Non-believers who die calmer than Muslims
outline.gist: He has seen people without faith meet death calmly; a Muslim cannot afford to leave mortality unaccepted.

outline.heading: Weakness from fear of death
outline.gist: The Prophet foretold a numerous but weak ummah crippled by love of the world and dislike of death; fear drove Adam's only mistake.

outline.heading: Outro

16:90.ar: ۞إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأۡمُرُ بِٱلۡعَدۡلِ وَٱلۡإِحۡسَٰنِ وَإِيتَآيِٕ ذِي ٱلۡقُرۡبَىٰ وَيَنۡهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلۡفَحۡشَآءِ وَٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَٱلۡبَغۡيِۚ يَعِظُكُمۡ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَذَكَّرُونَ
16:90.en: Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness, and giving to kinsfolk, and forbiddeth lewdness and abomination and wickedness. He exhorteth you in order that ye may take heed

16:91.ar: وَأَوۡفُواْ بِعَهۡدِ ٱللَّهِ إِذَا عَٰهَدتُّمۡ وَلَا تَنقُضُواْ ٱلۡأَيۡمَٰنَ بَعۡدَ تَوۡكِيدِهَا وَقَدۡ جَعَلۡتُمُ ٱللَّهَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ كَفِيلًاۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَعۡلَمُ مَا تَفۡعَلُونَ
16:91.en: Fulfil the covenant of Allah when ye have covenanted, and break not your oaths after the asseveration of them, and after ye have made Allah surety over you. Lo! Allah knoweth what ye do

16:92.ar: وَلَا تَكُونُواْ كَٱلَّتِي نَقَضَتۡ غَزۡلَهَا مِنۢ بَعۡدِ قُوَّةٍ أَنكَٰثࣰ ا تَتَّخِذُونَ أَيۡمَٰنَكُمۡ دَخَلَۢا بَيۡنَكُمۡ أَن تَكُونَ أُمَّةٌ هِيَ أَرۡبَىٰ مِنۡ أُمَّةٍۚ إِنَّمَا يَبۡلُوكُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦۚ وَلَيُبَيِّنَنَّ لَكُمۡ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ مَا كُنتُمۡ فِيهِ تَخۡتَلِفُونَ
16:92.en: And be not like unto her who unravelleth the thread, after she hath made it strong, to thin filaments, making your oaths a deceit between you because of a nation being more numerous than (another) nation. Allah only trieth you thereby, and He verily will explain to you on the Day of Resurrection that wherein ye differed

16:93.ar: وَلَوۡ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَجَعَلَكُمۡ أُمَّةࣰ وَٰحِدَةࣰ وَلَٰكِن يُضِلُّ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَهۡدِي مَن يَشَآءُۚ وَلَتُسۡـَٔلُنَّ عَمَّا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
16:93.en: Had Allah willed He could have made you (all) one nation, but He sendeth whom He will astray and guideth whom He will, and ye will indeed be asked of what ye used to do

16:94.ar: وَلَا تَتَّخِذُوٓاْ أَيۡمَٰنَكُمۡ دَخَلَۢا بَيۡنَكُمۡ فَتَزِلَّ قَدَمُۢ بَعۡدَ ثُبُوتِهَا وَتَذُوقُواْ ٱلسُّوٓءَ بِمَا صَدَدتُّمۡ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَلَكُمۡ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمࣱ‏
16:94.en: Make not your oaths a deceit between you, lest a foot should slip after being firmly planted and ye should taste evil forasmuch as ye debarred (men) from the way of Allah, and yours should be an awful doom

16:95.ar: وَلَا تَشۡتَرُواْ بِعَهۡدِ ٱللَّهِ ثَمَنࣰ ا قَلِيلًاۚ إِنَّمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ هُوَ خَيۡرࣱ لَّكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ تَعۡلَمُونَ
16:95.en: And purchase not a small gain at the price of Allah's covenant. Lo! that which Allah hath is better for you, if ye did but know

16:96.ar: مَا عِندَكُمۡ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقࣲۗ وَلَنَجۡزِيَنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ صَبَرُوٓاْ أَجۡرَهُم بِأَحۡسَنِ مَا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ
16:96.en: That which ye have wasteth away, and that which Allah hath remaineth. And verily We shall pay those who are steadfast a recompense in proportion to the best of what they used to do

16:97.ar: مَنۡ عَمِلَ صَٰلِحࣰ ا مِّن ذَكَرٍ أَوۡ أُنثَىٰ وَهُوَ مُؤۡمِنࣱ فَلَنُحۡيِيَنَّهُۥ حَيَوٰةࣰ طَيِّبَةࣰۖ وَلَنَجۡزِيَنَّهُمۡ أَجۡرَهُم بِأَحۡسَنِ مَا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ
16:97.en: Whosoever doeth right, whether male or female, and is a believer, him verily we shall quicken with good life, and We shall pay them a recompense in proportion to the best of what they used to do

aEi34jg4Ic8.speaker: adnan
aEi34jg4Ic8.speaker_note: Speaks of 'how I have been giving my khutbahs over the last years' and launches his own new series; single voice throughout after the Arabic opening.
aEi34jg4Ic8.title: Listening to the Divine: Al-Nahl 90-97
aEi34jg4Ic8.one_line: Launches a recite-and-translate khutbah series with An-Nahl 90-97 on justice and keeping covenants, prefaced by a call to respond to Sudan as to Gaza.
aEi34jg4Ic8.summary: He opens with a preface that has nothing to do with the series: the community mobilized for Gaza, so it must mobilize the same way for Sudan. He names a long-standing problem in the ummah, favoritism in whose suffering gets attention, and says Muslims from Africa, South Asia and China have accepted that nobody cares about them. The older generation has normalized ignoring certain crises; the children must learn to respond equally. He then introduces a new format: like the Prophet sometimes did, he will simply recite a passage, translate it slowly and explain it, because Muslims raised with the Quran have habituated listening without processing. The passage is An-Nahl 90-97, the verses that for some 1200 years have closed every Friday khutbah by a caliph's decree, and the verses that made Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah admit this was not human speech before Abu Jahl pressured him into calling it magic. He walks through them: three commands and three prohibitions, fulfilling the covenant, not unspinning the yarn, not treating oaths as instruments of personal interest, the foot that slips after standing firm, not selling Allah's covenant cheaply because what you hold runs out while what is with Allah remains, and the good life promised to the believer who does good.

outline.heading: Opening
Respond to Sudan as you did to Gaza
outline.gist: Before the series: the community answered the genocide in Gaza with real will to change, and it owes the same response to the crisis in Sudan. Sudan is the measure of a wider problem: favoritism in whose pain counts.

outline.heading: An ummah that ranks pain has no future
outline.gist: He grew up questioning why one Muslim crisis drew a response and a similar one elsewhere did not; any human crisis deserves a response, and an ummah that ranks its members' suffering cannot succeed.

outline.heading: Ask the forgotten
outline.gist: Muslims from parts of Africa, South Asia, China or Europe will say they have endured systematic oppression for decades, even a century, and have made peace with the idea that no fellow Muslim cares.

outline.heading: Feel for them as for your own
outline.gist: People in Sudan face circumstances you would never accept for yourself or a loved one; if that is how you feel about those close to you, you must feel it for those who are different.

outline.heading: Our children must respond equally
outline.gist: The older generation got used to responding to some regions and ignoring others; the children must react to a Muslim suffering in Afghanistan, Myanmar or China as they would to one in Sudan, Somalia, Syria, Iraq or Palestine.

outline.heading: Normalized struggles and the Gaza benchmark
outline.gist: People feel left out because some struggles were normalized and ignored. The advocacy, signs and giving shown for Gaza must be the same everywhere; they are not less. Dua for Sudan, Yemen, Afghanistan and the forgotten.

outline.heading: The Prophet's khutbahs of pure recitation
outline.gist: The Prophet would often stand on the minbar and give a khutbah that was only Quran: after his introduction he recited Surah Qaf in full by some narrations, or particular passages by others.

outline.heading: A weekly reminder of what the Divine expects
outline.gist: The point of the Friday gathering is that someone reminds the community of the Divine's teachings and the direction He wants; nothing does that better than listening to Him directly.

outline.heading: Habituated listening
outline.gist: Many raised with the Quran have learned to hear it without processing it the way they process ordinary speech; he has heard this for years from people, so the coming khutbahs will each take one passage.

outline.heading: The verse that closes every khutbah
outline.gist: He will recite slowly, then translate and explain, so people learn to listen. These verses are usually heard at the end of khutbahs because a caliph decreed that 16:90 replace something else said there, a practice of some 1200 years.

outline.heading: Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: not the speech of a human
outline.gist: Hearing these verses, al-Walid swore they were not human speech, fruitful above and abundant below, rising and never surpassed; under Abu Jahl's pressure he called them inherited magic.

outline.heading: Recitation of the passage
outline.gist: He recites An-Nahl 90 to 97 in full, slowly.

outline.heading: Justice, excellence and giving to kin; indecency, evil and oppression
outline.gist: Allah commands justice, ihsan and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing and oppression, admonishing so that you remember: three things you must do and three you must not.

outline.heading: Accepting the covenant
outline.gist: If you put out your hand and accept these terms, you have taken a covenant with Allah; do not break oaths after confirming them, having made Allah your guarantor, for He knows what you do.

outline.heading: The woman who unspun her yarn
outline.gist: An Arabian proverb: a woman who lost her mind spun firm yarn into strong fabric and then unspun it all. Do not build something firm and useful and then undo it yourself.

outline.heading: Oaths as instruments of interest
outline.gist: Taking oaths as deceit so that one group may be greater than another means entering a covenant corruptly, for personal interest rather than truth and righteousness.

outline.heading: May your word stand for something
outline.gist: Do not cherry-pick commitments by who is stronger or more useful to you; be a person of principle who stands by an oath because it is correct and just. Allah tests you by it.

outline.heading: Not forced into one nation
outline.gist: Had Allah willed He would have made one nation, with no rival groups to choose between; He chose not to compel anyone, into Islam or anything else.

outline.heading: Choice, and oaths driven by interest
outline.gist: His decree is that people choose; He lets astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. Do not let oaths and covenants be driven by corruption or the hunt for power and safety.

outline.heading: The foot that slips after standing firm
outline.gist: Changing loyalties out of interest, fear, greed or changed circumstances makes a foot that stood on principle slip, leaving only difficulty and distance from people and from Allah, with a great punishment.

outline.heading: Do not sell Allah's covenant for a small price
outline.gist: Do not give up the covenant for a cheap return; what is with Allah is better for you, and nothing else is.

outline.heading: What you hold runs out
outline.gist: Whatever you have, whatever it may be, will not last, because you yourself run out; nothing is worth more than holding to the covenant, which lasts forever because its source is the Divine.

outline.heading: What is with Allah remains
outline.gist: What is with Allah endures, and He will repay the patient by the best of what they did; then the promise to the believer, male or female, who does good.

outline.heading: A good life promised to the individual
outline.gist: Most of Allah's promises in this world are made to the collective; to the individual He promises only this, a good life, tayyibah from the root of goodness, and the best reward in the Hereafter.

outline.heading: Outro

32:2.ar: تَنزِيلُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ لَا رَيۡبَ فِيهِ مِن رَّبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
32:2.en: The revelation of the Scripture whereof there is no doubt is from the Lord of the Worlds

32:3.ar: أَمۡ يَقُولُونَ ٱفۡتَرَىٰهُۚ بَلۡ هُوَ ٱلۡحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ لِتُنذِرَ قَوۡمࣰ ا مَّآ أَتَىٰهُم مِّن نَّذِيرࣲ مِّن قَبۡلِكَ لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَهۡتَدُونَ
32:3.en: Or say they: He hath invented it? Nay, but it is the Truth from thy Lord, that thou mayst warn a folk to whom no warner came before thee, that haply they may walk aright

31:15.ar: وَإِن جَٰهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تُشۡرِكَ بِي مَا لَيۡسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلۡمࣱ فَلَا تُطِعۡهُمَاۖ وَصَاحِبۡهُمَا فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَا مَعۡرُوفࣰ اۖ وَٱتَّبِعۡ سَبِيلَ مَنۡ أَنَابَ إِلَيَّۚ ثُمَّ إِلَيَّ مَرۡجِعُكُمۡ فَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ

uuJlkVTsm84.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat As-Sajdah (Introduction, verses 1-3)
uuJlkVTsm84.one_line: Opening As-Sajdah: the surah closes the Quran's 'relationships' cluster with the most important one, the servant's relationship with Allah.
uuJlkVTsm84.summary: He opens Surat As-Sajdah, which the Prophet recited every Friday Fajr, by placing it at the end of a cluster running from Al-Qasas: relationships with people, with time, with the laws of creation, between generations, and finally with Allah. The word sajdah sums up that last relationship, which is a private secret of the heart. Like any relationship it can grow dull and mechanical, and it only holds when both sides invest; Allah has already given first, so the effort is now ours. He draws a practical rule: do not chase people who do not want you, except parents and the minimum due to kin. Happiness depends on relationships far more than comfort, as newcomers to Canada discover, and a sound relationship with Allah repairs all the others. The only worldly promise to an individual in the Quran is a good life, meaning inner fullness, not wealth or long life, which is why a barefoot child in Gaza has more dignity than the powerful who oppress him. He then explains his method of giving a compass for reflection, touches on the disjointed letters, and reads verses 1-3: revelation is Allah communicating, the relationship needs certainty with no doubt, and its purpose is guidance.

outline.heading: The Prophet's Friday Fajr recitation of As-Sajdah
outline.gist: He recited As-Sajdah and Al-Insan in full every Friday Fajr and prostrated in it, a sunnah the companions kept constantly.

outline.heading: The cluster of surahs on relationships
outline.gist: From Al-Qasas to As-Sajdah each surah treats one relationship: people, time, the laws of creation, generations, and lastly Allah.

outline.heading: Why sajdah sums up the relationship with Allah
outline.gist: Prostration of body, heart and mind captures the bond; unlike other relationships it is a hidden secret between the servant and his Lord.

outline.heading: When the relationship grows dull and mechanical
outline.gist: Relationships fluctuate; do not curse time, and beware of speaking to Allah with the tongue while the heart wanders. The dullness comes from our side, never His.

outline.heading: Both sides must invest, and Allah gave first
outline.gist: His nearness, love and pleasure match ours; He has already shown kindness through countless blessings, including bringing you to His house tonight.

outline.heading: The son of Adam who insults and repels his Lord
outline.gist: The hadith qudsi on people reviling Allah and making themselves hateful to Him through sin despite His favours shows a relationship only one side is mending.

outline.heading: Do not chase those who do not want you, except parents and kin
outline.gist: Parents are honoured regardless and kinship is kept at least at a minimum; otherwise leave people who reject you. A marriage also needs both spouses to want it.

outline.heading: Everything in the deen is this relationship
outline.gist: Prayer, dua, striving, obedience and sin are all the content of the bond with Allah; some surahs address such central topics more directly than others.

outline.heading: Surahs the Prophet kept reciting and the virtue of Friday
outline.gist: Al-Kahf, Al-Mulk, As-Sajdah and Al-Insan were recited regularly, a signal to pay close attention; Friday's merits explain why he started it with this surah.

outline.heading: Relationships are the secret of happiness
outline.gist: Newcomers to Canada have every comfort yet feel miserable because they lack family and friends; a king is lonely because he has only followers and rivals.

outline.heading: A sound relationship with Allah repairs every other one
outline.gist: Honouring parents, accepting hard laws of creation and bearing people all become acts of obedience to Him, so those close to Allah are content even in war and poverty.

outline.heading: Quality of life, not length or wealth
outline.gist: As medicine weighs quality of life against extra months, what matters is how one lives; people wrongly measure it by money, fame or career.

outline.heading: The only worldly promise to the individual: a good life
outline.gist: Promises to the community exist, but to the individual Allah promises only a good life, not health, wealth, children or protection from persecution.

outline.heading: What 'tayyib' means: a life filled from within
outline.gist: Like fruit that ripens when filled with water and sugar, a good life has no inner emptiness because one knows why he exists and accepts trials as tests.

outline.heading: Dignity of the oppressed in Gaza versus the fear of the oppressor
outline.gist: The powerful occupier lives afraid and mocked, while a barefoot child in Gaza is more honoured because he stands with truth; Abu Bakr told the Prophet he was good in life and death.

outline.heading: The relationship with Allah is a private secret
outline.gist: No one knows another's bond with Allah; Abu Bakr was distinguished by something settled in his heart, and those who know Allah recognise one another.

outline.heading: The method of these sessions: a compass for reflection
outline.gist: He leaves grammar and fiqh to the classical tafsirs and aims to show each surah's purpose so listeners can reflect correctly on their own, as his teachers sought insights even from students.

outline.heading: Alif Lam Mim as a thread linking surahs
outline.gist: The disjointed letters group surahs that share a theme; each surah has dimensions of revelation time, place in the mushaf, and what it gives you.

outline.heading: Revelation as Allah speaking to you
outline.gist: No relationship exists without communication; besides what He gives and takes in life, Allah addressed us directly by sending down a Book.

outline.heading: No doubt in it: certainty as the foundation
outline.gist: The relationship cannot stand if one doubts Allah or that the Book is His word; one must know who the other party is and accept His speech.

outline.heading: Answering the claim that he fabricated it
outline.gist: The verse confronts doubts spread by the weak of faith: it is the truth from your Lord.

outline.heading: The purpose of the relationship: guidance
outline.gist: Every relationship needs a defined aim; this one is so that people may be guided, and the Arabs had received no warner for centuries.

outline.heading: Outro
